# Diagnosing Overheating in LS1/LS2 Camaros: Beyond the Radiator Swap

Replacing a radiator, thermostat, and hoses on a high-output engine like the LS1 or LS2 is a significant financial commitment, yet it does not guarantee thermal stability. If your 1999â2002 C6 Camaro continues to climb past 210Â°F while the electric cooling fans remain silent, you are likely dealing with a control logic failure rather than a hydraulic restriction. The core issue isn't necessarily that the components are broken in isolation, but that the Electronic Control Module (ECM) is not receiving the signal required to activate the load circuitry.

In these platforms, the cooling fan system is not a simple on/off switch; it is a sequenced safety system managed by the Powertrain Control Module (PCM). The PCM monitors coolant temperature via the Engine Coolant Temperature (ECT) sensor and vehicle speed via the Vehicle Speed Sensor (VSS). When the ECT exceeds the threshold of approximately 210Â°F, the PCM should energize Relay 1 (low-speed fans) and Relay 2 (high-speed fans). If the gauge reads 210Â°F+ and both fans are dead, the failure point is almost exclusively electrical or software-related within the control loop.

### Verifying the Fan Control Circuit

Before replacing fuses, which is often a low-hanging fruit that yields nothing, you must verify the state of the PCM output. Populating the fuse box with new fuses will not fix an open circuit caused by a failed relay or a blown main fan fuse (F15 in many LS1 harnesses). The diagnostic path requires checking for 12V at the fan relay sockets when the engine is hot.

If you have access to a multimeter, back-probe the control side of the low-speed fan relay. If there is no voltage present despite the ECT sensor reading high, the PCM has not commanded the output. At this stage, the issue is internal to the computer or the input sensors feeding it. A common pitfall in Camaro overheating scenarios is assuming the thermostat is stuck open when it is actually closed too tightly, but a completely non-responsive fan system at 210Â°F points directly to the control module logic.

### The Role of Input Sensors

The PCM relies on specific inputs to trigger the fans. If the ECT sensor provides a voltage indicating "cold" even while the engine is boiling over, the PCM will not engage the fans. Similarly, on many LS models, the VSS signal is required for the high-speed fans to operate in certain driving conditions, though the low-speed fans should still activate based purely on temperature.

If you have already replaced the physical components and verified the relays are intact, the next step involves checking the data stream if you have a scanner capable of reading live PCM data. Look for the ECT sensor voltage or millivolts value. If the reading stays static at a low value while the coolant is clearly hot, the sensor itself is providing false data, tricking the PCM into thinking the engine is cold.

### Software Calibration and Relocation

Another frequent oversight involves software calibration. Some aftermarket performance chips or reflash services alter the fan activation thresholds. If your car has been flashed with a "stage 2" tune that prioritizes fuel economy or aggressive timing over thermal safety, the PCM may be programmed to delay fan engagement until higher temperatures are reached, risking engine damage. Ensure that any ECU tuning preserves the factory cooling logic defaults unless you have explicitly verified the new thresholds are safe for street driving.

Additionally, check the physical location of the coolant temperature sensor. On many LS1/LS2 engines, the sensor is located on the intake manifold near the throttle body. If the sensor line has been routed incorrectly or if the sensor itself has degraded over time despite replacement parts, the signal integrity may be compromised. A faulty sensor can mimic a cold engine condition, preventing the fans from ever spinning up.

Finally, consider the possibility of a blown main power fuse for the fan circuit. While less common than a relay failure, a single point of failure in the high-current path can disable the entire system. Always verify continuity from the battery through the main fuse block to the relays before concluding the PCM is at fault. If the electrical path is clean and inputs are valid, but the fans still do not run, you may need to reprogram the PCM or replace the unit with a known-good calibration file that enforces standard cooling curves.
